**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I saw the name *Elias Voss*, it was scrawled in jagged ink across a yellowed postcard, tucked between the pages of a well-worn novel. The handwriting was slanted, desperate—like the writer had been holding the pen too tightly, as if afraid the words might slip away before they could be written. I didn’t know then that the name would haunt me for years, that it would become a kind of second skin, a label I couldn’t shake, no matter how hard I tried.

Elias Voss was a man who didn’t exist. Or at least, that’s what I told myself. The truth was more complicated. He was a ghost in the margins of my life, a figure who appeared when I least expected him, always just out of reach. I met him in a café in Berlin, where the air smelled of old books and coffee that had gone cold. He was sitting at a corner table, reading a newspaper, his fingers tapping an erratic rhythm against the wood. I recognized him immediately—the way his hair fell just past his collar, the way his jawline was sharp enough to cut glass. He looked like a man who had been carved from stone and then left to weather.

“You’re staring,” he said, without looking up.

I froze. “I—I wasn’t staring.”

He finally glanced at me, and his eyes were the color of storm clouds over the Baltic Sea. “You were.”

I should have walked away. I should have told myself that this was just another coincidence, that names like Elias Voss were common in Germany, that I was being ridiculous. But something in the way he held himself—like he was waiting for the world to break—made me stay.

“Do I know you?” I asked.

He set the newspaper down. “Probably not.”

“Then why do I feel like I do?”

He smiled, but it didn’t reach his eyes. “Because you’re looking for someone who looks like me.”

I wanted to argue, to tell him that wasn’t true. But the words died in my throat. Because I *was* looking for someone. Someone who had disappeared twelve years ago. Someone who had left behind only a name and a half-remembered face.

Elias Voss was my brother.

---

The revelation hit me like a physical blow. I stumbled back, my chair scraping against the floor. The café erupted into applause—laughter, murmurs, the clink of cutlery. I turned to see a group of strangers watching me, their faces twisted in amusement. One of them clapped me on the shoulder. “You okay, *Schatz*? You look like you’ve seen a ghost.”

I didn’t answer. I couldn’t. Because I had.

Elias had been my older brother by three years. We were close—too close, some might say. He was the one who taught me how to ride a bike, who stayed up late reading to me when I was afraid of the dark, who laughed at my terrible jokes until my face ached. Then, one day, he was gone. No note, no explanation. Just a single sentence in a letter from our mother: *“He’s gone. I don’t know where. I don’t know why.”*

I spent years searching. I checked every missing persons report, every cold case file, every obscure corner of the internet where names like Elias Voss might surface. And then, one day, I found him. Or at least, I thought I did. A social media profile. A blurred photo from a concert. A comment thread where someone had posted, *“Anyone know where Elias Voss is? He’s my cousin, and I haven’t heard from him in years.”*

I reached out. I messaged him. I waited. And waited.

And then, nothing.

---

The man at the café table—*Elias Voss*—leaned forward. “You’re not the first person to ask me that.”

“What?”

“About who I am. About where I come from.” He exhaled, long and slow. “I don’t know. Not really.”

I wanted to scream. I wanted to shake him until the truth came pouring out. But I couldn’t. Because I knew, deep down, that he didn’t know either.

“You look like him,” I said, my voice raw. “You have the same eyes.”

He didn’t deny it. He just stared back at me, and for a moment, I saw my brother’s face in his—my brother’s smile, my brother’s sadness, my brother’s quiet strength.

“Do you remember him?” I asked.

Elias Voss shook his head. “I remember *me*. And that’s enough.”

---

I didn’t stay in Berlin that night. I left before dawn, my suitcase half-packed, my heart heavy. I didn’t know if he was my brother. I didn’t know if he ever would be. But I knew one thing: the weight of a name was heavier than I’d ever imagined.

Because names weren’t just words. They were promises. They were ghosts. And sometimes, they were the only thing keeping you from falling apart.

I drove home in the dark, the radio static, the road stretching endlessly ahead. I thought about Elias—about the real one, the one who had disappeared, the one who might still be out there, somewhere, waiting for me to find him.

And I thought about the man in the café, the one who looked like him, who carried his name like a secret.

I wondered if he was waiting for me too.

---

**The End.**

*(Or is it?)*
